fixes.explanation: A fisher on the sea? Somebody's got Abel out on a boat with a net, and I'm picturing the sheep waving from the shore. Genesis 4:2 says Abel was a keeper of sheep. His work is a flock, and that's the job that goes with his name.

That's right. Genesis 4:2 says Cain was a tiller of the soil, so he works the ground. Abel has the sheep and Cain has the soil. Tilling is turning the ground over so something can grow. Me, I turn dough over and hope for cookies. Cain's work gets him a harvest.

Grain is a farmer's kind of gift, baker, and that's why I understand the mix-up. But look at who brings what. Cain is the one who brought some of the fruit of the soil (Genesis 4:3). Abel, the shepherd, brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock (Genesis 4:4). Two brothers, two jobs, two different offerings. Don't hand Cain's basket to Abel!

Goshen! I like the confidence, baker. It's a real place in Genesis, but it shows up much later (Genesis 47:27), and Cain's already long gone by then. His story ends up somewhere else. Genesis 4:16 says he settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Wrong map, friend. Right book, though!

That's right. Genesis 4:17 says Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch. Enoch was born to Cain and his wife in that same verse. A whole city with the boy's name on it. I bet that boy never had to spell his name at a restaurant.

Adam is Cain's father, baker, and I get why his name jumped out first. He's the big name at the start of the chapter. But the city doesn't take his name. Genesis 4:17 says Cain named it after his son Enoch. Cain looked forward to the next generation, not back. If I named a bakery after somebody, it wouldn't be my dad's stamper either.
